KEY MESSAGE 1...Increasing warmth and humidity Sunday. 

Clouds and southerly flow across the area presently will promote
a milder night, with lows mainly in the upper 60s to lower 70s.
Sunday will be notably more humid, with most areas seeing dew 
points creep back into the low-mid 70s and actual temps again in
the mid-upper 80s. This will result in a day that feels warmer 
despite relatively minimal sunshine under thickening high and 
mid clouds. The next system approaching may bring some showers 
and storms into the area late, but most likely hold off until 
evening, so have generally held POPs below likely.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Showers and thunderstorms increase in coverage 
Sunday night into Monday with the potential for areas of heavy rain 
leading to a risk of flash flooding. There is also some risk for 
strong to severe thunderstorms.

An upper-level trough will shift across eastern Canada into early 
next week. While this occurs, strong energy crests a ridge in the 
West and this carves the trough out more into the Tennessee and Ohio 
valleys by later this weekend. There continues to be signals in 
model guidance showing this trough potentially becoming closed 
off into early next week as it gradually approaches the East. 
The main trough may detach and depart to the northeast leaving 
behind a lingering closed low. This scenario would lead to the 
system slowing its eastward progression through the first half 
of next week. The model trends continue to show a slower arrival
of this system, with the bulk of the showers and thunderstorms 
occurring later Sunday night and especially on Monday.

Ahead of the strengthening upper-level trough, deep south to 
southwest flow will increase and this will ramp up the low-level 
moisture and temperature advection. It will therefore be a humid 
time frame as the precipitable waters surge to 2+ inches. There 
looks to be multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms, starting 
with an initial round late Sunday night into Monday with the 
increased warm air advection regime. Instability will increase, 
however the timing at night should limit the thunderstorm intensity 
especially since it may be more of elevated convection initially. 
Areas of heavy rain however will be probable given the increasing 
forcing for ascent and high water content air. When looking at model 
soundings, the high precipitable water values, warm cloud layer 
processes, and tall skinny CAPE profiles show the heavy rain 
potential. For Sunday night into Monday, the Weather Prediction 
Center has us in a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) for
excessive rainfall. 

On Monday, ripples of energy along the incoming cold front 
during the day may enhance the convective potential and with deep 
southerly flow, some training convection will be possible. Excessive 
rainfall rates would enhance the flash flooding risk, especially 
from the I-95 corridor to the north and west where the elevation 
rise could boost the ascent some given a southeast to south low-
level flow. There is a Slight Risk (level 2 out of 4) for Excessive 
rainfall for Monday into Monday night for mainly northern portions 
of New Jersey. There is a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) for the 
rest of our area. 

In terms of the severe weather risk, uncertainty remains around the 
exact extent of instability present due to cloud cover and the round 
of showers/thunderstorms Monday morning. If enough heating develops 
during the course of Monday, then this combined with some increase 
in shear (some initially backed low- level flow) could lead to at 
least some severe thunderstorm risk. The Storm Prediction Center has 
highlighted areas near and north of Philadelphia in a Marginal risk 
(level 1 out of 5) for isolated severe thunderstorms with the 
primary risk being damaging wind gusts.

Beyond Monday night, the slow eastward progression of this system 
looks to keep the chance for convection going for multiple days next 
week as the cold front may stall in our vicinity. The current 
forecast does have shower and thunderstorm chances each day next 
week, mainly in the afternoon and evening. The most active day, as 
of now, however looks to be Monday given the overlap of favorable 
parameters for more widespread convective development.
